title: Social theories of disability
blurb: Use the social model, normalisation, social role valorisation and O'Brien's five accomplishments to plan care that removes barriers and builds valued lives.
question: Priya, 29, has a mild learning disability and wants to join her local gym. Staff at her supported living service say she 'won't cope with the machines' and suggest the day centre's exercise room instead. Which response best reflects social theories of disability?

teach.body: Models of disability are ways of thinking that shape how services act. The medical model locates disability in the person's impairment, which professionals diagnose and try to treat or fix. The social model locates disability in the barriers society creates (attitudes, environments, systems), which can be identified and removed. In plain English: is the person the problem, or is it the steps, the jargon and the rules?

teach.caption: The social model does not deny impairment or health needs; it shifts the focus to what can be changed around the person.

teach.body: Normalisation means making the ordinary patterns and conditions of everyday life available to people with learning disabilities: a home, a daily rhythm, work, leisure, relationships, as close as possible to those of everyone else in society. It developed in Scandinavia (Nirje) and was taken up in North America by Wolfensberger. It is about ordinary conditions of life, not about making people behave 'normally'.

Wolfensberger developed normalisation into social role valorisation (SRV). People who are devalued by society are at risk of rejection, segregation and poor treatment. Supporting them into socially valued roles (worker, neighbour, student, club member, volunteer) in ordinary settings improves how others see them and builds their skills. Grouping devalued people together, away from the community, reinforces devaluation.

teach.caption: Relationships are sometimes called community participation.

head: Accomplishment
Looks like
rows: Using local shops, GP, gym, library
Deciding clothes, food, activities, who supports you

teach.body: Person-centred planning, promoted by Valuing People (2001), puts the person at the centre: it starts with what is important to them and for them, involves the people they choose, and shapes support around their life rather than fitting them into existing services. Valuing People set four key principles: rights, independence, choice and inclusion. For nurses this connects to the NMC Code: treat people as individuals and respect their preferences.

The barrier is not Priya; it is a standard induction she may find hard to follow. The nurse talks with Priya and the gym about adjustments: a longer induction, pictures on the machines, a familiar staff member or a gym buddy at first. Using the local gym gives community presence, the chance of relationships, a valued role as a member, and new competence. The day centre room would keep her separate, which is what these theories warn against.

teach.text: Normalisation is NOT 'making people normal'. It is making ordinary life conditions available. And the social model does not mean ignoring health needs: treat the illness, remove the barrier.

items: Medical model: impairment is the problem. Social model: barriers are the problem and can be removed.
Normalisation (Nirje, Wolfensberger): ordinary patterns and conditions of everyday life.
SRV (Wolfensberger): support people into valued social roles in ordinary settings.
O'Brien: community presence, relationships, choice, respect, competence.
Person-centred planning: what matters to the person, with people they choose.

summary: You can now contrast the medical and social models of disability, explain normalisation and social role valorisation, use O'Brien's five accomplishments to judge a service, and apply person-centred planning to remove barriers rather than fitting people into services.

A.q: Rob, 41, has a moderate learning disability. His support now includes using the local library, barber and café each week, rather than activities on site. Which of O'Brien's accomplishments is this most directly developing?
options: Developing competence
Gaining respect
Community presence
Exercising choice
A.why: Community presence means sharing the ordinary places of community life: shops, cafés, libraries and services.

whyNot.1: Respect is about valued roles and how the person is seen.
whyNot.3: Choice is about control over decisions; the focus here is using community places.

A.q: A hospital sends all appointment information as long standard letters. Joanne, who has a learning disability, cannot read them and misses appointments. Under the social model, what is disabling her?
options: Her limited reading ability
Her learning disability diagnosis
Her family not reading the letters to her
The hospital's way of sharing information
A.why: The social model locates disability in barriers: here, inaccessible information that the hospital can change (easy read, phone calls, texts).

whyNot.0: Focusing on her reading is the medical model view.
whyNot.1: The diagnosis describes her impairment; the barrier is the letter format.
whyNot.2: Relying on family shifts responsibility away from the service that created the barrier.

A.q: A student asks where the idea of normalisation first developed before Wolfensberger took it up in North America. Which is correct?
options: Scandinavia
Australia
Southern Europe
Japan
A.why: Normalisation developed in Scandinavia (Nirje) and was taken up and developed in North America by Wolfensberger.

whyNot.1: Australia was not the origin of normalisation.
whyNot.2: Southern Europe was not the origin of normalisation.
whyNot.3: Japan was not the origin of normalisation.

B.q: Jordan, 25, has a moderate learning disability. With support he has learned to use his bus pass and cook a simple meal. Which of O'Brien's accomplishments is being developed?
options: Respect
Competence
Relationships
Community presence
B.why: Competence is about developing skills and abilities that matter in everyday life.

whyNot.0: Respect concerns valued roles and how a person is seen.
whyNot.2: Relationships concern friends, family and connections.
whyNot.3: Travel involves community places, but the focus here is learning skills.

B.q: In a supported living service, staff stop calling the adults who live there 'the kids' and begin using their names and age-appropriate language. Which accomplishment does this most directly support?
options: Choice
Competence
Respect
Community presence
B.why: Respect is about people being valued and seen as adults with dignity; childish labels devalue them.

whyNot.3: Community presence concerns use of ordinary community places.

B.q: A colleague says the social model 'ignores the health needs of people with learning disabilities'. Which reply is most accurate?
options: It holds that impairments are not real for people with LD
It accepts impairments may need treatment but targets barriers
It replaces health care with community activities and support
It treats health needs as the person's own responsibility
B.why: The social model does not deny impairment or health needs; it focuses attention on removing the barriers that turn impairment into exclusion.

whyNot.0: The social model does not deny that impairments exist.
whyNot.2: Health care remains essential; barriers to it are what the model highlights.
whyNot.3: The model places responsibility on society and services to remove barriers.

C.q: Priya, 29, has a mild learning disability and wants to join her local gym. Staff say she 'won't cope with the machines' and suggest the day centre's exercise room. Which response best reflects social theories of disability?
options: Work with the gym to adapt her induction and offer a buddy
Use the day centre room, where staff already know her well
Advise her to wait until her skills with equipment improve
Ask her GP to confirm she is fit before anything is arranged
C.why: Adapting the local gym removes the barrier (social model), gives community presence and a valued role as a member (SRV), and builds competence.

whyNot.1: A segregated setting keeps her apart from community life.
whyNot.2: Waiting for her to change places the problem in her, the medical model view.
whyNot.3: Nothing suggests a medical concern; this delays her choice without reason.

C.q: Ellis, 30, has a learning disability and loves gardening. Which plan most strongly reflects social role valorisation?
options: Gardening sessions with others from his day centre
A gardening project run on a hospital site
Joining the local allotment society as a member
Watching gardening programmes at home with staff
C.why: SRV supports people into valued social roles in ordinary settings: an allotment society member alongside other local people.

whyNot.0: Grouping devalued people together in a separate setting reinforces devaluation.
whyNot.1: A hospital site is a segregated, devaluing setting.
whyNot.3: This gives no social role or community presence.

C.q: A learning disability nurse is reviewing support plans. Which feature shows that a plan is person-centred?
options: It is written by the most senior professional
Goals come from the activities the service runs
It focuses on reducing the person's deficits
The person chooses who is involved in planning
C.why: Person-centred planning starts with what matters to the person and involves the people they choose.

whyNot.0: Professional authorship puts the service, not the person, at the centre.
whyNot.1: Fitting people into existing activities is service-led planning.
whyNot.2: A deficit focus reflects the medical model.

reteach.title: The ramp test
reteach.question: A wheelchair user cannot enter a building with steps. Is the problem the wheelchair or the steps? Now apply that to a person with a learning disability and a jargon-filled letter.

blocks.body: The social model asks: what in the environment, attitude or system stops this person? For the wheelchair user it is the steps; for a person with a learning disability it may be a jargon letter, a rushed appointment or staff who talk to the carer instead. Remove that, and the person can take part.

blocks.text: O'Brien's five: Presence, Relationships, Choice, Respect, Competence. 'Independence' is a Valuing People principle, not one of the five accomplishments.

explain.body: Medical: impairment is the problem, professionals fix it. Social: barriers are the problem, society removes them.

test.q: Four managers describe how they would support Kerry, who finds the day centre timetable hard to follow. Which statement reflects the medical model of disability?
options: 'We will add picture symbols to the timetable'
'Staff will learn the signs Kerry uses'
'Kerry needs therapy so she can fit our routine'
'We will move her session to suit her bus times'
test.why: The medical model locates the problem in Kerry and tries to change her to fit existing arrangements.

whyNot.0: Adding symbols removes a barrier: social model.
whyNot.1: Staff learning her signs removes a communication barrier.
whyNot.3: Changing the timetable adapts the service to Kerry.

explain.body: Making ordinary patterns and conditions of everyday life available: home, routine, work, leisure, relationships. Not making people behave 'normally'.

test.q: A support worker says normalisation means 'teaching people with learning disabilities to act normally so they fit in'. Which description is accurate?
options: Providing treatment that reduces their differences
Making ordinary patterns and conditions of life available
Housing people in groups with similar support needs
Asking people to follow the routines of the service
test.why: Normalisation is about making the patterns and conditions of everyday life available, close to those of mainstream society.

whyNot.0: Normalisation is about life conditions, not treatment.
whyNot.2: Grouping by need is what normalisation challenged.
whyNot.3: It concerns society's ordinary patterns, not service rules.

explain.body: Wolfensberger: support devalued people into valued roles (worker, neighbour, student, volunteer) in ordinary settings, improving how they are seen and their skills.

test.q: Hayley, 33, has a moderate learning disability and loves animals. Which plan best reflects social role valorisation?
options: Animal sessions at her day centre each week
A volunteer role at the local animal rescue
Pet care tasks with staff in her own home
A pet therapy group for disabled people
test.why: A volunteer role at an ordinary community organisation gives Hayley a socially valued role.

whyNot.0: A segregated setting gives no valued community role.
whyNot.2: Helpful, but it gives no wider valued role.
whyNot.3: A disability-only group keeps people apart from the community.

explain.body: Community presence, relationships (participation), choice, respect and competence: what good services help people achieve.

test.q: Imran, 45, used to have staff decide his outings. Now each morning he picks from photo cards the place he wants to go. Which accomplishment is being developed most directly?
options: Choice
Competence
Respect
Community presence
test.why: Offering options and supporting Imran to decide develops choice: control over everyday decisions.

whyNot.1: No new skill is the focus; deciding is.
whyNot.2: Respect may benefit, but the direct focus is choice.
whyNot.3: Outings involve community places, but the change described is who decides.
